title: Zohran Mamdani’s NYC Tech Team Is What DOGE Should Have Been
gist: New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani launched Public Interest Technology (PIT) Crews — five small engineering teams working 12-week sprints inside city agencies, funded with $5.24 million plus a $2 million Rockefeller Foundation grant and run by USDS veterans under CTO Lisa Gelobter. Steven Levy argues it revives the 2014 US Digital Service playbook with an anti-Big-Tech inversion, and it is drawing talent: over 3,000 applicants for roughly 35 lower-paying, no-equity slots in the first week.

insights.claim: New York City's Public Interest Technology program consists of five teams of engineers and designers embedded with city agencies to rapidly build specialized apps that fix specific city-service problems.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: In-house municipal build capacity is a direct substitute for consultant and systems-integrator contracts — a structural threat to govtech vendors if it works.
insights.locator: PIT will consist of five “game-changing” teams

insights.claim: The PIT program operates on a budget of $5.24 million plus an additional $2 million grant from the Rockefeller Foundation that funds one of the five crews.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: A ~$7 million total against a city budget of this scale means the program is a proof-of-concept whose survival depends on demonstrable wins, not on funding inertia.
insights.locator: Her budget for the program is $5.24 million

insights.claim: PIT crews are structured to make their case by shipping working software in frantic 12-week sprints, positioning them as the mayor's operational counter to self-interested consultants and inefficient contractors.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: A 12-week delivery cadence gives an unusually short feedback loop for judging whether in-house civic engineering beats procurement — results will be visible within a quarter.
insights.locator: Seen that way, the PIT crews are essentially Mamdani’s symbolic stand-ins

insights.claim: The program's leadership frames technology as the enforcement layer of policy rather than a support function, on the view that unimplemented policy is inert.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: If regulation depends on shipped software to bite, then the delivery team — not the legislature — becomes the variable that determines whether a rule affects companies.
insights.quote: Without technology, policy is just words written on a piece of paper
insights.locator: The projects Gelobter and her team choose to tackle

themes.theme: USDS lineage and the DOGE contrast

insights.claim: The pitch behind PIT closely mirrors the one Barack Obama's chief technology officer Todd Park delivered in 2014 to recruit Silicon Valley talent into what became the United States Digital Service.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: The playbook has a twelve-year track record to evaluate against, so its known failure modes — political capture, talent churn — are the risks to watch here.
insights.locator: Because Mamdani’s message could have fit quite comfortably in the pitch

insights.claim: The USDS survived the first Trump administration and the Biden term, but in 2025 Elon Musk and DOGE infiltrated the agency and shut down much of its useful work, with the Trump administration now ostensibly reviving parts of it through the National Design Service.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Federal civic-tech capacity was dismantled and is being rebuilt under a different brand, leaving municipal programs as the credible near-term venue for this kind of work.
insights.locator: The agency somehow survived the first Trump administration

insights.claim: NYC's tech leadership is staffed by USDS alumni: CTO Lisa Gelobter served at USDS embedded in the Department of Education leading the College Scorecard, and both people she hired to run PIT — Luke Farrell and Maya Israni — are USDS veterans.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: The dispersed USDS alumni network is the transmission mechanism moving federal civic-tech practice into city governments — watch other large cities recruit from the same pool.
insights.locator: Mamdani’s transition team set the stage

insights.claim: Gelobter explicitly frames the effort as recreating the USDS experience and asserts an engineering-operator identity rather than an administrative one.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Leadership that can evaluate technical work directly is the single biggest differentiator between civic-tech programs that ship and those that procure.
insights.quote: I know how to build software
insights.locator: Gelobter says she brings an engineering mindset

insights.claim: Norm-breaking dress code is deployed deliberately as a cultural signal inside city government, echoing USDS's earlier fights with bureaucrats who refused to meet anyone in a hoodie.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Cultural friction, not technical difficulty, is the historical failure point for these programs — the visible signaling is a proxy for how much institutional resistance is expected.
insights.quote: I’m wearing jeans to work—not because I don’t look great in a suit, but it’s a statement, right?
insights.locator: It’s also a cultural thing for her

insights.claim: The first PIT crew project implements Mamdani's click-to-cancel regulation, announced July 10, which penalizes companies that make it difficult to cancel subscriptions or ongoing payments.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: A city-level subscription-cancellation mandate with enforcement tooling behind it is a direct margin risk for any consumer subscription business with New York customers.
insights.locator: On its face, the first project of the PIT crew seems nonintuitive

insights.claim: The click-to-cancel rule takes effect October 1, the same date the PIT crew plans to launch software letting citizens report services that obstruct cancellation.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: October 1 is a hard, dated catalyst — a crowdsourced whistleblowing pipeline turning on simultaneously with the rule converts it from paper into enforcement immediately.
insights.locator: The rule takes effect on October 1

insights.claim: Gelobter says the click-to-cancel project is expected to save roughly $160 million for New Yorkers and confirms it was designated a mayoral priority.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: That $160 million is revenue currently captured by subscription businesses through cancellation friction — the size of the pool being redistributed if the rule works.
insights.quote: It will show that we can directly affect people’s lives. It’s supposed to save, like, $160 million for New Yorkers
insights.locator: The city hasn’t yet announced what the other four PIT crews

insights.claim: Levy expects the remaining four PIT crews to focus on nuts-and-bolts city services with at least one addressing housing, while noting the first project's choice deliberately signals ordinary people standing up to bullying corporations.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: The unannounced crews are the option value — a housing-focused build would have far larger economic consequences than a subscription tool.
insights.locator: The city hasn’t yet announced what the other four PIT crews

themes.theme: Talent flows away from Big Tech

insights.claim: Over 3,000 people applied for roughly 35 PIT crew slots in the first week after the jobs were posted, with a shocking number coming from people currently in high-salaried big tech jobs despite the city roles paying considerably less with no equity.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: An ~86:1 application ratio at a large pay cut is a hard signal that senior engineering labor is repriceable by mission — relevant to retention costs at the incumbents losing them.
insights.locator: Farrell says that in the first week after the city posted

insights.claim: Israni reports that many applicants are disillusioned with the private tech industry and originally entered tech wanting to apply it for good, and Levy links the surge to techies seeking alternatives to developing AI that might decimate the labor force.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Ideological attrition driven by AI-displacement anxiety is an emerging, underpriced retention risk for AI labs and large platforms.
insights.quote: We've heard from a lot of folks recently who are disillusioned with the private tech industry and maybe went into tech because they wanted to apply tech for good
insights.locator: That message seems to be resonating among techies

insights.claim: The 2026 version of civic tech inverts the 2014 premise: where the Obama-era USDS sought to borrow Silicon Valley's prestige, Mamdani's program embraces Silicon Valley expertise while taking a skeptical, almost adversarial stance toward Big Tech itself.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Tech skill has decoupled from tech-industry prestige in progressive politics — a durable shift that shapes how future regulation and public-sector hiring are framed.
insights.locator: Even though much of Hizzoner’s personal tech surge is based on the USDS playbook

insights.claim: Mamdani publicly admitted he is subscribed to a service he cannot cancel because he does not know his login while the company holds his credit card details, an anecdote used to ground the click-to-cancel policy in a universal consumer grievance.
insights.speaker: Steven Levy
insights.so_what: Policies grounded in near-universal consumer friction are politically durable and likely to be copied by other cities and states.
insights.quote: I am currently subscribed to something I don’t even know my login for, but they have my credit card information, and I don’t know how to cancel it.
insights.locator: Mamdami might be the first customer
